Adam Stenavich.blurb: Stenavich's system in Green Bay doesn't lean heavily on any one structural feature — pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and screens all sit right at league average. The modest edge is in pre-snap motion (47% vs. a 41% norm) and a slightly elevated RPO rate, but neither is dramatic. What stands out is the output: +0.07 EPA/play ranks 12th across 82 play-callers, well above the league average of -0.01 — though it's worth being straight that those results came almost entirely with Jordan Love, so separating the scheme's value from the quarterback driving it isn't really possible yet.

Andy Reid.blurb: Reid's Kansas City offense passes more aggressively than almost anyone — +6.1 over expected, fifth in the sample — and backs it with a heavy screen game (10%, well above the 7% norm) and RPO usage that ranks second overall at 4% against a 2% average. Pre-snap motion at 50% adds another layer above the 41% league rate, while play-action and tempo sit right at average. The scheme value reads as middle of the pack, though with Patrick Mahomes in the equation that number can't be cleanly trusted; what's clearer is the output: +0.06 EPA/play, comfortably above a negative league average.

Ben Johnson.blurb: Ben Johnson's system sits at +0.093 scheme value, the best mark in this index, built on a play-action rate of 26% — well above the 18% league norm — and a creativity score of 61 that ranks sixth overall. Tempo is legitimately fast at 82 plays per game against a 75-play average, though pass tendency and motion are both ordinary. He almost never uses RPOs, which is a deliberate choice, not an oversight — the offense is structured, not menu-driven.

Brian Schottenheimer.blurb: Schottenheimer's Dallas offense is about as close to league average as a system gets — motion, play-action, RPOs, screens, and creativity all sit right at the norm. What stands out is tempo, running at 81 plays per game against a league average of 75, and a scheme value that grades out indicatively well at +0.061 against a league average of -0.012, though that number carries a caveat: it's hard to fully disentangle from the quarterback running it. The results land in the middle of the pack at +0.05 EPA/play, which fits a system that wins, if it wins, through volume and execution rather than anything exotic.

Drew Petzing.blurb: Petzing's Detroit offense is about as close to the league mean as a system gets — pass tendency, screens, RPO usage, and creativity all sit right at or within a hair of average. The two places it nudges above the norm are play-action (22% versus an 18% league average) and pre-snap motion running slightly *below* the norm (35% against 41%), which is a mild surprise for a team associated with an up-tempo identity. Scheme value is middling at +0.014, results are modestly positive at +0.02 EPA/play — a functional, unflashy operation that gets the job done without leaving much of a distinctive fingerprint.

Jim Bob Cooter.blurb: Cooter's Indianapolis offense was about as conventional as it gets on most dimensions — motion, screens, tempo, and overall creativity all sit right at the league median. The clearest departures are a play-action rate of 23% (well above the 18% norm) and a slight lean away from passing relative to expectation, suggesting a run-first orientation that fed those play-fakes. Results landed just below average at -0.03 EPA/play, which is ordinary rather than damaging.

Kellen Moore.blurb: Moore's system is about as average as it gets across most dimensions — creativity, pass tendency, play-action, and screens all sit right at league norm. The two things that stand out are pre-snap motion at 50% (against a ~41% league average) and a slightly higher tempo at 79 plays per game, which together suggest he's trying to create leverage before the snap rather than through exotic play design. Results land just below league average at -0.02 EPA/play, but scheme value comes in at -0.002 against a league average of -0.012, meaning the system itself is holding its own even where the raw output hasn't.

Kevin O'Connell.blurb: O'Connell runs a genuinely creative offense — 57th percentile on exoticness, top-12 historically — built around heavy play-action at 24% of dropbacks, well above the 18% league norm, with everything else sitting right at league average. The honest read on results, though, is that the scheme grades out below average on both EPA/play and adjusted scheme value, which means the stylistic identity hasn't consistently translated into production. This is a system worth watching as it accumulates more signal across different roster configurations.

Kyle Shanahan.blurb: Shanahan's system sits near the top of the league in adjusted scheme value — +0.091 against a league average of -0.012 — and the results back it up at +0.13 EPA/play, both elite marks. The defining structural feature is pre-snap motion on 60% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm, which is the engine that creates the leverage his offense runs on. Everything else — play-action at exactly 18%, tempo, screens, RPOs — sits right at league average, meaning the edge isn't exotic volume, it's what the motion unlocks before the snap.

Matt LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's system doesn't have a defining wrinkle — the creativity score, motion rate, play-action, tempo, and pass tendency all sit within a few points of league average. What it does have is a +0.076 scheme value and +0.07 EPA/play, both well above average, though both numbers come with an asterisk: this offense ran through Aaron Rodgers and then Jordan Love, and separating the system from the quarterback is genuinely difficult. The honest read is a clean, competently run scheme that produces, with the source of that production still somewhat open to debate.

Matt Nagy.blurb: Nagy's Giants offense sits close to league average on most structural dimensions — tempo, motion, play-action, and creativity all land in the middle of the pack. What actually stands out is a strong pass-over-expected lean (third-highest tendency in the sample) and an unusually high RPO rate at 4%, more than double the league norm. The scheme value reads as mildly positive, though with moderate reliability it's indicative at best given the quarterback dependency baked into those four seasons. Results have been slightly above average.

Mike LaFleur.blurb: LaFleur's Arizona offense sits close to league average on most dimensions — creativity, tempo, screens, and pass tendency are all within a few ticks of normal — but pre-snap motion is a genuine outlier at 53% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm, ranking ninth among 82 coaches. RPOs are essentially absent (1%, against a 2% average), so the motion isn't serving a read-option system; it's about creating conflict pre-snap in a more traditional structure. Results came in at +0.04 EPA/play, modestly above average, but the scheme ran with effectively one quarterback, so how much of that belongs to LaFleur versus his QB isn't something the data can answer cleanly.

Mike McDaniel.blurb: McDaniel runs one of the most structurally active offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 61% of dropbacks (league norm is 41%) and a creativity score that ranks third among 82 coaches — but the results haven't matched the design, with offensive EPA and scheme value both sitting below average. The one clear tension: he runs noticeably less than expected given his personnel tendencies, ranking 68th in pass-run balance, while leaning on screens at nearly double the league rate (11% vs. 7%). The style is genuinely unusual; the production, so far, isn't.

Sean McVay.blurb: McVay's system runs on pre-snap motion (54% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm) and play-action (23% vs. 18% league average) — two levers he's pulled consistently to create leverage before the ball is snapped. The creativity score sits right at the middle of the pack, so the edge isn't exotic design; it's disciplined execution of a system that's slightly pass-heavy and almost entirely free of RPOs. Scheme value comes in at +0.050, indicative of a real edge, though with the same quarterback for much of this run, that number is hard to hold too precisely.

Sean Payton.blurb: Payton's Denver offense runs close to league-average on most dimensions — tempo, play-action, motion, and overall pass tendency all sit right at the norm. Where he actually deviates is in screens (10%, versus a 7% league average) and RPOs (3%, modest but above average), which together suggest a system that leans on horizontal release valves more than most. The scheme value comes in at +0.018 against a league average of -0.012, which is a real positive, though results land right at break-even EPA — a gap worth watching as the roster matures.

Shane Steichen.blurb: Steichen runs a conventional scheme by most measures — motion, tempo, screens, and pass tendency all sit near league average — but two elements stand out: play-action at 23% (against an 18% norm) and a scheme value of +0.034 against a league average of -0.012, good for 12th of 82 callers. The results so far, -0.03 EPA/play, are below average, which suggests the system's underlying value hasn't translated yet in Indianapolis.

Todd Monken.blurb: Todd Monken's offense ranks seventh among 82 play-callers in QB- and opponent-adjusted scheme value at +0.056, well above the league average of -0.012 — and almost nothing else about it stands out structurally. Motion, play-action, tempo, screen rate, RPO usage: every dimension sits right at the league norm. The results are good (+0.06 EPA/play, 17th overall), but the value here is coming from execution and design quality, not from doing anything structurally unusual.

Wes Phillips.blurb: Phillips ran a fairly conventional offense in Minnesota — most of his markers sit right at league average. The one real signature is play-action: he used it on 24% of dropbacks, well above the 18% league norm, which fits a system that leaned on the run game to create passing opportunities. Results were below average at -0.06 EPA/play, though separating scheme value from personnel across four seasons in Minnesota is its own complication.

Zac Taylor.blurb: Zac Taylor runs one of the more pass-heavy systems in the league — +8.8 over expected pass rate ranks second among 82 coaches — while keeping almost everything else near the median: motion, tempo, play-action, and screen usage all sit right at league average. The creativity score of 39 out of 100 confirms it: this isn't a scheme that wins through structural cleverness, it wins through volume and execution in the passing game. The QB-adjusted scheme value of +0.036 against a league average of -0.012 suggests the system itself is adding real value, not just riding talent.

Bobby Slowik.blurb: Slowik's offense ranks among the more exotic in the league structurally — 57th percentile on creativity, pre-snap motion at 47% against a 41% norm — but the results land squarely in the middle, with EPA/play at -0.04 against a league average of -0.01. Play-action, tempo, and screens all sit right at league norms, and he actually runs the ball slightly more than expected given down-and-distance context. The scheme value of -0.057 against a league average of -0.012 suggests the system isn't generating much extra worth on its own.

Brad Idzik.blurb: Idzik's offense in Carolina sits close to league average on almost every dimension — pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all land within a point or two of the norm. The one real deviation is pre-snap motion, which he uses on just 33% of dropbacks against a league average of 41%, making this a notably static offense pre-snap. Scheme value comes in slightly positive at +0.017, though with only moderate reliability it's better read as "not hurting the team" than a confirmed edge; results bear that out with EPA/play essentially at zero.

Dan Pitcher.blurb: Dan Pitcher's offense has one defining trait that separates it from nearly everyone else: he passes more than any play-caller in the sample, running +8.9 over expected pass rate against a league average of -1.1. Everything else — motion, tempo, play-action, RPOs — sits right at the median, and his scheme is among the least exotic in the league at 38/100. The honest caveat is that those results (+0.07 EPA/play, 13th overall) came with a specific quarterback situation in Cincinnati, so how much is Pitcher and how much is the talent around him remains an open question.

Frank Smith.blurb: Frank Smith runs one of the more structurally active offenses in the league — pre-snap motion on 70% of dropbacks (league average is 41%, and no one ranked higher) and screens at nearly double the league rate combine to create a system built around manufacturing leverage before and immediately after the snap. Play-action at 25% (versus 18% league average) fits the same logic: make the defense declare, then attack. Pass tendency sits right at league average, results came in around neutral, and the system produced that with an approach that genuinely deviated from the norm.

Joe Brady.blurb: Brady's offense sits in the middle of the pack on most surface-level tendencies — pass rate, play-action, RPO, tempo — so the results don't come from doing unusual *things*, they come from pre-snap architecture: motion on 52% of dropbacks against a league norm of 41% puts him in the top 12. The creativity score of 64 (league average 50, top 4 overall) reflects genuine structural variety, not just personnel rotation. Scheme value of +0.041 is indicative of a real edge, though it can't be cleanly separated from the quarterback situation, so the +0.17 EPA/play — second in the league — is the more honest receipt.

Joe Lombardi.blurb: Lombardi's Denver offense leaned on play-action (24%, against an 18% league average) and screens (12%, more than double the 7% norm) as its primary tools — a structure built around creating easy reads and manufactured space rather than raw scheming complexity. RPO usage was also notably high at 4%. The results landed right at league average, which is roughly what the style suggests: a functional, complementary system without a strong signature in either direction.

Klint Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's system lands in genuinely interesting territory: a creativity score of 57 puts him in the top 15% of play-callers leaguewide, driven largely by pre-snap motion on half of all dropbacks — well above the 41% norm — while nearly everything else sits at or near league average. The scheme value is a modest positive at +0.011 against a league average of -0.012, and the offense produced essentially neutral EPA/play, so the results back up a system that's quietly functional rather than flashy. He runs the ball slightly more than expected and almost never uses RPOs, which at 1% is about as low as it gets.

Liam Coen.blurb: Coen's system sits almost exactly at league average across every structural dimension — motion, tempo, play-action, screen rate, RPO usage — which makes the output numbers genuinely striking: +0.088 scheme value (third among 82 callers) and +0.11 EPA/play rank sixth overall. The honest read is that this isn't a scheme winning on exoticness; it's a conventional framework executing at an unusually high level, and the QB-adjusted scheme value says the system itself, not just the personnel, is doing real work.

Nathaniel Hackett.blurb: Hackett's Arizona offense was about as conventional as it gets — pre-snap motion at 30% against a league norm of 41%, almost no RPOs, and creativity that ranks 73rd of 82 callers. Pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and screens all sit right at league average. The results were poor (-0.10 EPA/play, well below the -0.01 norm), but the scheme value lands in the middle of the pack, which suggests the personnel was doing more damage than the design.

Press Taylor.blurb: Press Taylor's Chicago offense was about as close to league-average as a system gets — pass tendency, play-action, tempo, and results all sit right at the norm. The one genuine deviation is pre-snap motion at 32%, well below the ~41% league average, suggesting a simpler, more static approach to alignment. Scheme value comes in at -0.001, slightly above the league average of -0.012, but with only moderate reliability given the quarterback context, so that number is indicative at best.

Zac Robinson.blurb: Robinson's most notable tendency is a strong lean toward the run — passing 8 percentage points below expectation, well below the league norm of roughly 1 point under, putting him among the most run-heavy play-callers in the sample. Beyond that, the system is largely conventional: motion, tempo, play-action, and screens all sit near league average. Scheme value comes in at -0.021 against a league average of -0.012, which is a real gap, though results have tracked similarly middling, leaving the picture consistent if unimpressive.

Alex Van Pelt.blurb: Van Pelt runs the fastest-paced offense in the sample — 86 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and that's genuinely the defining feature of the scheme. Everything else sits near the middle: conventional motion, ordinary play-action, almost no RPOs, slightly elevated screen usage. The problem is the results: -0.11 EPA/play ranks 68th, well below the -0.01 league average, suggesting the volume hasn't translated to value.

Arthur Smith.blurb: Arthur Smith runs a run-heavy, play-action-forward system — 23% play-action rate against an 18% league average, and a pass rate that sits well below expectation. The screen game is a real differentiator at 10% (league avg 7%), giving him a horizontal release valve to pair with the downfield fakes. Everything else — creativity, motion, tempo — lands right at the norm, and the results match: average EPA, average scheme value. It's a coherent if unspectacular identity built on leverage from the run threat.

Declan Doyle.blurb: Doyle's offense is genuinely creative — a 61/100 exoticness score ranks fifth among 82 play-callers — but almost everything else sits right at league average: motion at 42%, play-action at 20%, tempo at 73 plays per game, all within a rounding error of the norm. The creativity shows up in structure and design, not in leaning on any single tool. Results are solid at +0.05 EPA/play, and scheme value reads as slightly above average, though with only moderate reliability it's worth treating as directional rather than definitive.

Doug Nussmeier.blurb: Nussmeier's Saints offense was about as close to league-average as an NFL scheme gets — pass tendency, tempo, motion, and RPO usage all sit right at the norm. The one meaningful deviation is a low screen rate (4% against a 7% league average) and a below-average play-action rate (13% vs. 18%), suggesting a relatively conventional, structure-first approach. Results came in at -0.06 EPA/play, modestly below the league average of -0.01, though two seasons in New Orleans carries enough roster context that the number tells only part of the story.

Eric Bieniemy.blurb: Bieniemy's KC offense was notably pass-heavy — +7.2 over expected, fourth among 82 coordinators — while keeping most other dials close to league average: motion at 31% (below the 41% norm), play-action at 15% (below 18%), and tempo a tick slower than average. The results were ordinary on paper at +0.01 EPA/play, but that number, like everything here, can't be separated from the quarterback — with Patrick Mahomes running the operation, what belongs to the scheme and what belongs to the player is genuinely unknowable.

Grant Udinski.blurb: Udinski's Jacksonville offense doesn't stand out stylistically — motion, play-action, tempo, and screen usage all sit right at or near league average, and he almost never touches RPOs. What stands out is the results: +0.10 EPA/play ranked seventh out of 82 qualifiers against a league average of -0.01. A conventional scheme that produced at an elite level is worth noting, even if the how isn't particularly exotic.

Greg Roman.blurb: Roman's system in Los Angeles is defined by two things above almost everything else: play-action at 27% of dropbacks — second in the league against an 18% norm — and pre-snap motion on 52% of snaps, well above the 41% average. Everything else sits close to league average: tempo, screens, RPOs, overall creativity. The scheme value reads as a mild positive, but with only moderate reliability given the QB overlap, and the results — +0.01 EPA/play — are essentially middle of the pack, so the style is clearer than the verdict.

Josh McDaniels.blurb: McDaniels' system in New England reads almost entirely conventional on paper — motion, play-action, RPOs, and tempo all sit right at league average, and his creativity score of 49 is exactly middle of the pack. What stands out are the edges: screens well below the league norm (4% vs. 7%) and an +0.11 EPA/play that ranks fifth overall. The scheme-value number (+0.083, indicative rather than precise given the sample) suggests the system is producing real value, though it's hard to fully disentangle from the quarterback running it.

Ken Dorsey.blurb: Dorsey runs one of the fastest-paced offenses in the league — 85 plays per game against a 75-play average, ranking second overall — and leans pass-heavy at +2.5 over expected, but nearly everything else sits squarely at league norm. The speed hasn't translated into production: -0.04 EPA/play against a -0.01 average, with a scheme value of -0.060 that ranks 44th. Volume and tempo are real, results aren't.

Klay Kubiak.blurb: Kubiak's offense in San Francisco was built on pre-snap motion — 52% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm — and leaned pass-heavy relative to game script, sitting at +2.8 over expected while almost never touching RPOs (effectively 0% against a 2% average). Play-action and tempo were both ordinary. What makes the profile notable is the results: +0.13 EPA/play ranked third of 82, though with one elite quarterback running the system, how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the player isn't cleanly separable.

Klayton Adams.blurb: Adams ran one of the more conventional offensive systems in the league — motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sit within a rounding error of league average — but the results were genuinely strong, ranking 9th of 82 in EPA/play at +0.09 against a league average of -0.01. The honest caveat: he no longer calls plays, and Dallas's offensive environment makes it hard to know how much of that production was scheme versus personnel.

Kliff Kingsbury.blurb: Kingsbury's Washington offense is defined by two things that genuinely stand out: play-action on 26% of dropbacks (league average is 18%, top four in the sample) and RPOs on 4% (double the norm, also top four). Those aren't incidental — they're the structural core of how he creates leverage at the line of scrimmage. Tempo is real too at 82 plays per game, and scheme value sits at +0.032 against a league average of -0.012, with the results backing it up at +0.07 EPA/play. Motion and pass tendency are both close to average, so this isn't an everything-at-once system — it's built on a few specific stresses applied consistently.

Luke Getsy.blurb: Getsy runs a genuinely up-tempo offense — 83 plays per game ranks eighth in the sample against a league average of 75 — and pairs that pace with pre-snap motion on 51% of dropbacks, well above the 41% norm. Everything else sits close to average: play-action, screens, RPOs, and pass tendency are all within a few ticks of the league. The results have been poor (-0.10 EPA/play, 64th of 82), and the scheme itself grades out below average at -0.049 against a league mean of -0.012, so the volume and movement haven't translated.

Mike Kafka.blurb: Kafka's Giants offense runs fast — 83 plays per game puts him in the top tier of tempo callers — but speed hasn't translated to production, with a -0.14 EPA/play that ranks 72nd and a scheme value sitting below league average. Everything else is essentially ordinary: motion, play-action, RPO usage, and screen rate all land right at or near the norm. The honest read here is that the structure isn't unusual enough to be the story — the results are.

Mike McCarthy.blurb: McCarthy's Pittsburgh offense is about as conventional as it gets — creativity, motion, play-action, tempo, and RPO usage all sit right at or below league average, with nothing that stands out in either direction. The one genuine tendency is a slight lean toward passing more than the situation calls for, ranking 12th in pass rate over expected. The results haven't justified it: -0.07 EPA/play against a league average of -0.01, and a scheme value of -0.041 that ranks 36th of 82 — below average even after accounting for quarterback and opponent context.

Nick Caley.blurb: Caley's Houston offense is about as close to the league mean as a system gets — motion, tempo, play-action, pass tendency, and overall creativity all sit right at or within a tick of average. The one real deviation is screens, where he calls them at 4% against a 7% league norm, making that a notably absent tool. Results land just above average at +0.01 EPA/play, though the scheme value reads slightly below average and carries only moderate reliability, so how much of that is the system versus the quarterback remains genuinely unclear.

Nick Holz.blurb: Holz runs a run-heavy, conventional offense — pass rate nearly 6 points below expectation puts him among the league's most committed rushing teams, and the scheme itself is straightforward, sitting below league average on creativity. The results have been poor: -0.14 EPA/play ranks 71st, and the scheme value of -0.094 against a league average of -0.012 suggests the system itself isn't adding much beyond the personnel. RPOs and screens show up slightly more than average, but nothing here deviates enough to call it a defined identity — it's a vanilla run-first approach that isn't generating the efficiency to justify the commitment.

Shane Waldron.blurb: Waldron's system doesn't have a strong signature except for one: screens, which he deploys on 12% of plays, well above the 7% league average and a top-4 rate across the sample. Everything else sits in the middle — motion, play-action, tempo, and pass tendency all land near league norms, and the scheme's overall creativity index (44/100) is slightly below average. The scheme value of -0.038 against a league average of -0.012 is a modest drag, and the -0.03 EPA/play bears that out.

Tim Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Giants offense runs faster than most — 82 plays per game against a league norm of 75 — and leans heavily on play-action (24%, 6 points above average) and screens (10%, well above the 7% norm). Pre-snap motion is actually light at 32% versus the 41% league average, so the scheme creates stress through volume and play-design more than pre-snap complexity. The results land squarely in the middle, and the adjusted scheme value does too, which makes this a coherent but unexceptional system so far.

Tommy Rees.blurb: Rees runs one of the more run-heavy systems in the league — 7.1 percentage points below expected pass rate, well below the -1.1 league norm — but the approach isn't generating much. Atlanta's offense sits at -0.14 EPA/play, 73rd of 82 callers, against a league average of -0.01. Motion (34%) and RPOs (1%) are both below average, and scheme value comes in at -0.102 versus the -0.012 norm, though two seasons is a short window. The style is conventional and ground-oriented; the results, so far, haven't justified it.

Andrew Janocko.blurb: Janocko's Raiders offense ran at a noticeably slow pace — 63 plays per game against a league average of 75 — and stripped out most of the complementary wrinkles: play-action at 11% (league average 18%), screens at 4% (league average 7%), and effectively no RPOs. The creativity score of 57 sits in the top 10, which suggests the exoticness came from something other than those conventional tools, though one season of data makes it hard to draw firm conclusions. Results landed just above average at +0.02 EPA/play, which is functional without being definitive.

Brian Angelichio.blurb: Angelichio's Pittsburgh offense was a study in subtraction — almost no motion (21%, against a league norm around 41%), almost no play-action (8% vs. 18%), and a deliberately slow tempo (62 plays per game vs. 75). The one genuine outlier was pass tendency: seventh in the league at +3.6 over expected, so he was willing to throw, just without much pre-snap wrapping paper. Results landed right at league average, which is about as far as you can read into one season of data.

Brian Daboll.blurb: Daboll's Tennessee offense is one of the more deliberately stripped-down systems in the league — low motion (21%, versus a ~41% norm), minimal play-action (10% against an 18% average), and a slow pace that ranks near the bottom at 56 plays per game. The results have been below average at -0.09 EPA/play, though with one quarterback driving the entire sample, there's no clean way to separate what's scheme from what's signal-caller — so that number tells you something, just not exactly what.

Brian Fleury.blurb: Fleury runs one of the more stationary, deliberate offenses in the league — pre-snap motion at 24% and play-action at 11% both sit well below the league norms of 41% and 18%, and Seattle plays at a noticeably slow pace. What makes it interesting is that the creativity score (57/100, above average) suggests the plays themselves aren't conventional, even if the pre-snap packaging is sparse. Scheme value reads slightly below average, though with only moderate reliability it's better treated as a rough signal than a verdict.

Chip Kelly.blurb: Kelly's Las Vegas offense runs heavy pre-snap motion (56% of dropbacks, well above the 41% league norm) and play-action at an unusually high rate (25% vs. 18% average) — both signatures of a system designed to manipulate defensive alignment before the snap. Everything else sits near league average, and the results were poor (-0.21 EPA/play, 76th of 82). The scheme-value estimate is moderately reliable at best, so how much of that is Kelly and how much is the quarterback situation is a fair question, but the production numbers don't offer much to argue with.

Dave Canales.blurb: Canales runs a conventional system by most measures — motion, pass tendency, play-action, and screens all sit right around league average — with two genuine outliers: tempo near the top of the league at 81 plays per game, and an RPO rate of 4% against a 2% league norm. The creativity score (40/100, well below the 50 average) suggests the volume comes from execution of a tight, familiar playbook rather than schematic variety. Results landed at essentially league average EPA/play, though the system ran almost entirely with one quarterback, so how much of that belongs to the scheme itself can't be cleanly answered.

David Blough.blurb: Blough's Washington offense is defined less by what it does and more by what it doesn't — play-action at 10% against an 18% league average, pre-snap motion at 25% against 41%, screens and RPOs essentially nonexistent. The result is a bare-bones, deliberate system that runs fewer plays per game than almost anyone (62 vs. a 75-play norm). Scheme value sits in the middle of the pack, though with only one season of data it's indicative at best; the EPA output lands exactly at league average, which for a system this stripped-down is at least not an indictment.

Davis Webb.blurb: Webb's Denver offense was defined more by what it didn't do than what it did. Play-action at 10% (league average is 18%), pre-snap motion at 24% (league average 41%), and a tempo of just 56 plays per game (league average 75) all rank near the bottom of the league — this was a deliberately stripped-down operation. Results landed roughly at league average at -0.02 EPA/play, which is neither a vindication nor an indictment of the approach.

Frank Reich.blurb: Reich's Jets offense was about as conventional as it gets — low motion (18%, versus a league norm around 41%), minimal play-action (9% against an 18% average), and a deliberately slow pace that ranked near the bottom of the league. The scheme barely uses pre-snap manipulation of any kind. What makes this hard to read clearly is that the system ran with effectively one quarterback, so whatever scheme value exists can't be separated from that quarterback's own contribution — the +0.04 EPA/play that ranked 23rd leaguewide could reflect the QB as much as the design.

John Morton.blurb: Morton's Detroit offense runs with a notably distinct pre-snap identity — motion on 59% of dropbacks and play-action on 26% of snaps both rank fifth in the league against averages of 41% and 18%, and a 10% screen rate adds another layer of manufactured advantage before the ball is snapped. The system also runs at a high pace (82 plays/game, 12th) while leaning run-heavy, sitting well below the league pass tendency norm. Results were strong at +0.08 EPA/play, but with one quarterback driving the whole window, how much of that belongs to the scheme versus the player genuinely can't be separated.

Josh Grizzard.blurb: Grizzard's system runs faster and moves more than almost anyone in the league — 84 plays per game and pre-snap motion on 58% of dropbacks both rank in the top 10, against averages of 75 and 41%. He also leans on screens at twice the typical rate.
